meta.title: ACCT 321 — Worked Example Set 2: Service Corporation — Month 2
meta.description: A corporation providing services. Introduces credit transactions, accounts receivable, accounts payable, unearned revenue, and prepaid expenses. Students practice recording transactions that involve credit rather than immediate cash.
learning_objectives: Record services performed on account (accounts receivable)
Record receipt of cash from customers on account
Record unearned revenue (cash received before service)

transactions.description: On March 1, TechSolve Inc. issued common stock and received $100,000 cash from investors.
transactions.explanation: For a corporation, owner investments are recorded in Common Stock (and possibly Additional Paid-in Capital if above par value). Cash increases (debit) and Common Stock increases (credit). Unlike a sole proprietorship, the corporation does not use Owner's Capital.

transactions.description: On March 2, purchased office supplies for $1,500 on account (credit terms: net 30).
transactions.explanation: Purchasing on account means the business receives the supplies now but pays later. Supplies (asset) increases with a debit, and Accounts Payable (liability) increases with a credit. The liability represents the obligation to pay in the future.

transactions.description: On March 5, performed services for a client and billed $4,000 on account.
transactions.explanation: When services are performed but cash is not yet received, the business records Accounts Receivable (an asset). Accounts Receivable increases with a debit, and Service Revenue increases with a credit. The revenue is earned even though cash hasn't been collected.

transactions.description: On March 7, received $2,500 cash from a customer for services to be performed in March and April.
transactions.explanation: Cash received before services are performed creates a liability called Unearned Revenue. The business owes the customer future services. Cash increases (debit) and Unearned Revenue increases (credit). Revenue is NOT recorded yet — it will be recorded when the services are actually performed.

transactions.description: On March 10, paid $600 cash for a one-year insurance policy effective March 1.
transactions.explanation: Insurance paid in advance is a prepaid expense — an asset because the business will receive future benefit. Prepaid Insurance increases (debit) and Cash decreases (credit). Each month, $50 ($600 ÷ 12) will be moved from Prepaid Insurance to Insurance Expense.

transactions.description: On March 12, received $4,000 cash from the client billed on March 5.
transactions.explanation: When the customer pays their account, Cash increases (debit) and Accounts Receivable decreases (credit). Note: No revenue is recorded here — the revenue was already recorded on March 5 when the service was performed. This is just the collection of cash.

transactions.description: On March 15, paid $1,500 cash to the supplier for the supplies purchased on March 2.
transactions.explanation: Paying an account payable reduces both the liability and cash. Accounts Payable decreases with a debit, and Cash decreases with a credit. The expense was not recorded at purchase — supplies become an expense when consumed.

transactions.description: On March 20, performed services for a client and received $3,200 cash immediately.
transactions.explanation: Cash service revenue — the simplest revenue transaction. Cash increases (debit) and Service Revenue increases (credit). The revenue is earned at the same time cash is received.

transactions.description: On March 25, paid $2,000 cash for employee salaries.
transactions.explanation: Salaries Expense increases with a debit, and Cash decreases with a credit. Salaries are an operating expense that reduces net income and therefore reduces retained earnings.

transactions.description: On March 28, the board declared and paid $2,000 cash dividends to shareholders.
transactions.explanation: Dividends are distributions of earnings to shareholders. Dividends is a contra-equity account (normal debit balance) that reduces Retained Earnings. Dividends increase with a debit, and Cash decreases with a credit. Like Owner's Drawings for a sole proprietorship, Dividends are NOT an expense.

key_takeaways: Corporations use Common Stock (not Owner's Capital) and Dividends (not Owner's Drawings)
Revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash is received (accrual basis)
Accounts Receivable = revenue earned but cash not yet collected
Unearned Revenue = cash received but revenue not yet earned (a liability)
Prepaid expenses are assets, not expenses, until consumed
Paying an accounts payable reduces both the liability and cash — no expense is recorded
Collecting accounts receivable swaps one asset (receivable) for another (cash)
